paras: The bombing of a flat building on Indiana Avenue was an explosion in early 1919 that wrecked a three-story brick building at 3365-3401 Indiana Avenue on the South Side of Chicago, a building tenanted by Black families in an otherwise white block. Six-year-old Ernestine Ellis was killed and several members of the households living there were injured. First reports left the cause open between a dynamite bomb and defective gas pipes, but Black papers later counted it among a series of bombings of Black homes, and it figured in a June protest to Mayor William Hale Thompson.

According to the wire report, the wrecked building was tenanted by "Colored people," while all other houses in the vicinity were occupied by whites. A St. Louis Argus account in April explained that Black families had moved into formerly white districts of the South Side after the start of the war, and that some had refused to leave as rents rose.

The explosion went off just as Charles Thomas, son of the building's owner, was unlocking the front door, and it threw him into the street. The occupants were hurled from their beds, and Ernestine Ellis was thrown against the ceiling on the third floor, fracturing her skull and breaking her legs and arms. She was still alive when rescuers reached her but died on the way to a hospital.

Those listed as injured included the owner, C. A. Thomas, his wife Jennie and several of their children, Sanford Washington and his son Alexander, and Mrs. Emma Head, all bruised. Neighbors and victims said they smelled gunpowder after the blast, and the odor of escaping gas was thought to come from pipes broken by the explosion.

Police were described as "mystified" and were questioning residents of the neighborhood to learn whether race prejudice was responsible, while the gas company sent repair men to look for the origin of the explosion. No report of an arrest or inquest appears in the coverage.

In early June, according to the Chicago Broad Ax, Col. Richard E. Parker, Ida B. Wells-Barnett, Kathryn Rutherford and Mrs. Emma Head formed a committee and called on Mayor Thompson about the bombing of Black homes on the South Side, and the mayor refused to see them. The Broad Ax identified Mrs. Head as the woman "whose little child was killed" by a bomb in her home at 3365 Indiana Avenue.

The first account was a single wire dispatch dated Chicago, March 6, which the St. Louis Argus credited to the Associated Negro Press and the Dallas Express to the Associated Press. The Black weeklies printed it with headlines of their own: the Argus ran "Dynamite Kills 3 and Injures 6," although its text named only one death, the Cleveland Advocate added "Suspicion Rests on Whites," and the Richmond Planet, which printed it twice in one issue, called it "Bombed Colored Flat in Chicago." The dispatch itself took no side on the cause.

Later Black-press reports treated the blast as part of a campaign against Black residents. When bombs struck Jesse Binga's office and Alex J. Robinson's home in late March, the Argus called it "the third bombing of houses occupied by Negroes in the last three weeks" and named Ernestine Ellis's death among them. The Broad Ax went further, describing the bombers as "half devils and half savages," calling the child's death one of the most damnable crimes against childhood in the city, and blaming the Thompson administration and the police.

The date is uncertain: the wire dispatch of March 6 placed the explosion "early today," "early Monday" or "early Saturday" depending on the printing, while the Broad Ax, three months later, gave January 28, 1919. The Argus's April count of three bombings in three weeks fits the March date better. The sources also differ on the child's family, since the wire named the dead girl Ernestine Ellis and listed Mrs. Head only as bruised, while the Broad Ax called the child Mrs. Head's own.

reader.title: Bombing of a flat building on Indiana Avenue, Chicago
bases: An explosion, reported as a dynamite bomb or possibly defective gas pipes, wrecked a Black-tenanted flat building and killed a child; the Broad Ax called it a bomb thrown into a Black home (A1, A2, A10).

A wire dispatch carried by several Black papers and an independent local Chicago Broad Ax report agree that a child was killed by an explosion at 3365 Indiana Avenue, though they disagree on the date and the wire left the cause open (A1, A2, A10).

accounts.label: Wire report (Associated Negro Press / Associated Press)
accounts.gist: A dynamite bomb or defective gas pipes wrecked the Black-tenanted building in a white neighborhood, killing six-year-old Ernestine Ellis and injuring others; police were mystified and asking whether race prejudice was the cause, and neighbors smelled gunpowder.

accounts.label: Chicago Broad Ax
accounts.gist: A bomb exploded in Mrs. Emma Head's home at 3365 Indiana Avenue on Jan. 28, 1919, killing her child, one of a series of bombings of Black homes that the mayor had not condemned.

framing.detail: The wire story was reported without comment and left the cause open ('dynamite bomb or defective gas pipes'), though the Cleveland Advocate headlined 'Suspicion Rests on Whites' and the Richmond Planet 'Bombed Colored Flat in Chicago'.
The Broad Ax called the child's death 'one of the most damnable crimes' against childhood in the city and blamed Mayor Thompson and the police.

conflicts.note: The wire dispatch, closest in time, places the explosion in early March 1919, and later reports counting it among three bombings in three weeks before March 26 fit that; the Broad Ax date comes three months later and may reflect a misdating, but the coverage does not settle it.
